start.title: Every Club File Is Locked
start.bestWhy: Disconnect the infected machine from the network immediately to stop the spread, then find the root cause from evidence. Do not pay the ransom.
start.text: Monday morning. You open the club activity registration website you manage, and find that every file on the club's server is inaccessible. The member list of 1,000 people and the camp application forms are all encrypted and locked. A ransom note on screen demands 50,000 baht within 48 hours in exchange for the decryption key. The club camp starts in three days. What do you do first?
start.source: CISA #StopRansomware Guide; UK NCSC: Mitigating malware and ransomware attacks

choices.label: Immediately disconnect the infected machine from the internet and the local network, preserve the evidence, then investigate what happened.
choices.out: You take the registration website offline for about a day. Some members can't apply for the camp in time, but the ransomware doesn't spread to other club machines and you have the evidence needed to find the root cause.
u: Website down for a day — some members miss the camp application window.
choices.lesson: Contain first: ransomware spreads across networks. Disconnecting the infected machine quickly limits the damage. Then find the root cause from evidence.

choices.label: Pay the ransom to get the files back as fast as possible before the camp starts.
choices.out: You receive a key, but it only decrypts some of the files — and the attacker still has access through the original entry point.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Paying the ransom doesn't guarantee you'll get your files back, and it doesn't close the hole the attacker used to get in. International cybersecurity agencies advise against paying.

choices.label: Reset passwords on all club accounts — you think it was just a credential leak.
choices.out: Members scramble to set new passwords, but the files are still encrypted. The logs you read later reveal the attacker entered through an account nobody was using anymore.
u: Forced password reset — some members stop engaging.
choices.lesson: Base your hypothesis on evidence, not guesses. Fixing the wrong thing wastes time while the attacker is still inside the system.

choices.label: Delete everything and rebuild the entire club website and system from scratch.
choices.out: You spend two weeks rebuilding. The camp has to be postponed and many members drift away during the wait — but the new system definitely won't have the old ransomware on it.
u: Camp postponed — many members lost.
choices.lesson: Starting fresh looks safe but is extremely costly. And if you don't know how the attacker got in, the new system could be compromised the same way.

investigate.title: How Did the Attacker Get In?
investigate.bestWhy: There are two root causes — both must be closed: disable unused accounts, and keep backups on a separate system.
investigate.text: From the logs (system activity records) you find that the attacker logged in using an account belonging to a senior member who graduated the previous year. That account was still active and used the same password as one leaked from another website. There are two root causes: (1) old accounts were never disabled, and every account had full admin privileges; and (2) the backup files were stored on the same machine, so they were encrypted too. Only a copy from two weeks ago survives on a disconnected external drive. How do you fix this?
investigate.source: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (Protect: access and account management); CISA: 3-2-1 backup

choices.label: Disable all unused accounts, grant admin privileges only to those who need them, restore data from the disconnected backup, and set up an automated backup system on a separate machine that you actually test.
choices.out: You spend one day restoring data, ask members to re-enter the last two weeks of registrations, close 14 old accounts, and set up automated backups to a separate location — then test the restore. It works.
u: Members need to re-enter some of their information.
choices.lesson: Two key principles: grant only the minimum necessary access (least privilege) and disable accounts immediately when someone leaves. Backups must be stored separately from the main system — and you must actually test restoring them.

choices.label: Disable old accounts first — set up a proper backup system after the camp.
choices.out: Old accounts are closed and the website is back up quickly, but backup files are still stored on the same machine as the main system.
u: Brief website outage.
choices.lesson: A half-fix creates a false sense of security. If you get hit again, there's nothing to restore from.

choices.label: Restore data and set up a separate backup first — leave the old accounts alone because you're not sure who they belong to.
choices.out: Data is restored and you have a separate backup now — but the senior member's account that the attacker used is still active.
u: Brief website outage.
choices.lesson: Not knowing who an account belongs to is a reason to disable it, not a reason to leave it open.

partialClient.title: Hit Again — Nothing to Restore
partialClient.bestWhy: Backups must be separate from the main system and actually tested. Otherwise one attack wipes out everything.
partialClient.text: Five days later, a committee member opens an attachment in an email that looks like a camp T-shirt price quote. A new ransomware strain encrypts the files again — including the backup that was stored on the same machine. All camp registration data is gone.

u: Camp registration data lost — members must register again.

partialClient.source: CISA #StopRansomware Guide (offline, encrypted backups); UK NCSC: Backing up your data

choices.label: Set up automated backups to a separate location with multiple versions and test the restore — then teach committee members to be cautious with email attachments.
choices.out: This time you have to ask all members to register again, but from now on, even if the files get locked again, you can restore everything within an hour.
u: Website taken down to apply the fix.
choices.lesson: The 3-2-1 rule: keep 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with at least 1 copy off-site. A backup you've never tested isn't a backup you can trust.

choices.label: Copy files to a flash drive plugged permanently into the server.
choices.out: It looks like you have a backup — but a drive that stays plugged in is part of the machine. The next ransomware strain encrypts it along with everything else.
u: Backup gets encrypted too.
choices.lesson: A backup that's always connected to the machine will go down with the machine. It must be genuinely separate.

partialRules.title: Member List Leaked
partialRules.tag: Repeat Attack: Old Account Still Active
partialRules.bestWhy: Close the hole completely right away, check what data leaked, and notify members so they can protect themselves.
partialRules.text: Five days later, the attacker returns through the senior member's account that's still active. This time they don't lock files — they copy out the names, phone numbers, and school names of all 1,000 members, then threaten to publish the data unless they're paid. Some members start receiving strange calls.

u: Members receiving strange calls — some leave the club.

partialRules.source: EU GDPR Articles 33–34 (data breach notification); CISA #StopRansomware (extortion threats)

choices.label: Disable all unused accounts, check the logs to see what data was taken, then notify members and the faculty advisor directly — including advice on how to watch out for scammers.
choices.out: You message every member explaining what data leaked and warning them about calls claiming to be from the club. Some parents are upset, but many thank you for telling them quickly.
u: Some members leave after being notified.
choices.lesson: Notifying affected people quickly gives them a chance to watch out for scammers. (International data protection law such as the EU's GDPR requires notifying affected individuals when the risk is high.)

choices.label: Quietly disable the old account and don't tell anyone — you don't want the club's reputation to suffer.
choices.out: Things look normal at first, but members receiving strange calls have no idea where their data came from, so they can't protect themselves.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Staying silent doesn't bring the data back — it just leaves affected people without the ability to protect themselves, and the truth will come out eventually.

choices.label: Take the website down and ask the school's IT department or an external expert to audit the whole system before making any announcement.
choices.out: The expert finds two more insecure accounts and confirms exactly what data was taken. You announce with a clear remediation plan — but the website has to stay down for a long time.
u: Extended website outage — some members don't wait.
choices.lesson: External experts are valuable when you're unsure of the damage scope — but you need to weigh that against the time your service has to stay down.

repeat.title: Hit Again
repeat.bestWhy: Being hit again means the root cause is still there. Stop, fix everything properly, and communicate honestly.
repeat.text: Less than a week later, the club's files are locked again, and the attacker sends a sample of the member list as a threat. The original entry point is still open, and data may already be out. What do you do?

choices.label: Temporarily take the website down, disable unused accounts, set up a separate backup, then announce honestly to members what happened.
choices.out: You fix both root causes completely and announce the situation honestly. Members are upset, but most see that you're taking responsibility.
u: Website down — some members lost from the news.
choices.lesson: Being hit again means the first round didn't fix the root cause. Stop, review the evidence, fix everything completely, and communicate straightforwardly.

choices.label: Fix the system completely but don't tell members — you don't want to alarm them before the camp.
choices.out: The system is genuinely more secure — but members whose data leaked don't know, and aren't watching out for scammers.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: Concealing an incident doesn't protect anyone — it only delays the day the truth comes out.

choices.label: Switch to paper-based registration and leave the website as-is for now.
choices.out: The camp can proceed, but the still-open website remains an entry point for the attacker to return — and the old data in it continues leaking.
u: Some members register on paper.
choices.lesson: Avoiding the problem without fixing the system is leaving the door open for the attacker.

rewrite.title: New Site, New Holes
rewrite.tag: New Vulnerabilities from a Rushed Build
rewrite.bestWhy: Close the admin panel vulnerabilities before going live — multiple layers (login rate limiting + a second factor) are safer than waiting for something to go wrong.
rewrite.text: Two weeks later the new club website launches. Everyone has their own account, and there's a separate backup system. Some members return to register for the new camp round — but in the rush, you forgot to change the admin panel's default password (admin / 1234) and didn't limit failed login attempts. A bot (automated program) is now trying to guess the admin password about 3,000 times per hour.

u: Some members return to register for the new round.

rewrite.source: CISA Secure by Design (no default passwords); NIST SP 800-63B (limit login attempts)

choices.label: Change the default password, enable two-factor authentication (2-step) for the admin account, and limit failed login attempts.
choices.out: The bot keeps trying but gets blocked after just a few failed attempts — and even if it guesses the password right, it still can't get in without the code from your phone.
u: Members feel confident as the website stays stable.
choices.lesson: Defence in depth: rate limiting + a second factor means a weak or leaked password is no longer a single point of failure.

choices.label: Only change the default password to a longer one.
choices.out: A longer password helps a lot, but the bot can still try an unlimited number of times — and there's still no second factor if the password is phished.
u: No immediate effect.
choices.lesson: A strong password is a good first layer — but it shouldn't be the only layer.

choices.label: Don't do it right now — need to promote the camp first.
choices.out: First-day registrations are great — but that night the bot successfully guesses the admin password.
u: Promotion pays off.
choices.lesson: A risk that hasn't materialized yet is not a risk that doesn't exist. A bot actively guessing passwords is clear evidence the website is already being targeted.

wave2.title: A Message from a Fake Teacher
wave2.bestWhy: Verify through a channel you know yourself — not a link in the message — and add a second factor to important accounts.
wave2.text: About a week passes. The previous entry points are closed, but the attacker changes tactics. You receive a chat message from an account using the faculty advisor's photo and name, saying: "I need to approve the camp budget urgently today — can you log in through this link for me?" The link looks exactly like the club website's login page.
wave2.source: CISA Secure Our World: Recognize and Report Phishing; UK NCSC: Phishing attacks

choices.label: Don't click the link. Call the advisor directly at their known number to confirm, and enable 2-step for all admin accounts.
choices.out: The advisor never sent that message. You recognize it as phishing, enable 2-step for all admins, and warn the committee not to click links like this.
u: Website stable — members return.
choices.lesson: A message creating urgency + claiming to be someone you trust + a link is the classic phishing signal. Always verify through a channel you already know.

choices.label: Click the link and log in — it's the advisor asking.
choices.out: That page is a fake that captures your password. A few hours later someone logs into the club website's admin panel using your credentials.
u: No visible effect yet.
choices.lesson: Attackers love impersonating people we respect or trust — because we act before we think.

choices.label: Ignore the message and delete it.
choices.out: You dodge this one — but you didn't warn anyone else on the committee, and there's still no second factor. If someone else falls for it, there's nothing to stop the attacker.
u: No additional incidents.
choices.lesson: Not being fooled this time doesn't mean the team is safe. Warn others and add a second factor.

takeover.title: Admin Account Hijacked
takeover.bestWhy: You need to cut the attacker off from every access point — not just change the password. Then audit what they changed, and warn members immediately.
takeover.text: The attacker is inside the club website's admin panel using a legitimate admin account. They changed the camp payment link to their own bank account and viewed member data. Several students have already transferred money.

u: Payment link altered — many members lost.

takeover.source: NIST SP 800-61 (incident response); OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet

choices.label: Log out every active session on all devices, change passwords on all accounts, enable 2-step, audit the logs for what was changed, restore the payment link, and warn members immediately not to transfer money.
choices.out: You go through every change, close every access point, and immediately notify members and the advisor. The damage stops there.
u: Website down for remediation — some members leave after being notified.
choices.lesson: When an account is hijacked, you must cut the attacker off from every access point — including active sessions (logins still in progress). Then warn users as fast as possible.

choices.label: Change the password only, then reopen the website.
choices.out: The attacker is still logged in on their device. They come back the next night and change the payment link again.
u: Brief downtime to change the password.
Attacker returns via the still-active session.
choices.lesson: Changing the password alone isn't enough. If the attacker still has an active session, they can keep coming back. You must log them out of every device.

choices.label: Ask the school's IT department or an external expert to audit the entire backend, then follow their recommendations.
choices.out: The team discovers the attacker created a hidden admin account. They remove it, set up 2-step, and members are notified. Slow, but thorough.
u: Extended outage — some members don't wait.
choices.lesson: Attackers often leave a "backdoor" behind. Expert eyes can find things you'd miss — but it comes at a cost in time.

news.title: The Story Spreads Through the Student Group
news.bestWhy: If you missed the disclosure window, admit it and act as soon as you realize. The longer you stay silent, the more trust you lose.
news.text: A student posts that someone called them claiming to be from the club, knowing their name, phone number, and school — and tried to trick them into transferring money. The post spreads through student chat groups thousands of times, and everyone starts asking whether the club knew about this.

u: News breaks that the club covered up the incident.

news.source: EU GDPR Article 34 (notification of affected individuals)

choices.label: Issue a public statement acknowledging the incident, explaining what data leaked, what has been fixed, and warning members to watch out for scammers.
choices.out: You admit you knew earlier and didn't notify anyone. The criticism is heavy — but the clear information helps members protect themselves, and some still stay.
u: Some members leave after learning they were kept in the dark.
choices.lesson: If you missed the disclosure, fix it the moment you realize. Late transparency is still better than none.

choices.label: Say it has nothing to do with the club.
choices.out: Students cross-reference the details and find they match the club's camp registration form. The denial gets shared as an example of irresponsibility.
u: Caught denying verifiable facts.
choices.lesson: Denying verifiable facts turns a data incident into a full-blown credibility crisis.

choices.label: Take the website down for three days to investigate before making any announcement.
choices.out: You confirm the full scope of the damage before speaking — but during those three silent days, the rumours spread further than the facts.
u: Three days of silence — rumours spread.
choices.lesson: Verifying before speaking is good — but if you go silent too long, rumours will tell the story for you.

wave2_blocked.title: Phishing That Failed
wave2_blocked.text: The following week, a fake message impersonating the faculty advisor reaches club committee members. One committee member already entered their password on the fake page — but the attacker can't get into the account, because every admin account has 2-step enabled. You receive an alert about a login attempt from an unknown device.

u: Members see the website running smoothly — no incidents.

wave2_blocked.source: Microsoft Security: MFA blocks nearly all automated account takeovers; CISA Secure Our World

choices.label: View summary
choices.out: You change that committee member's password and remind the team to stay alert. No damage is done.
u: No damage.
choices.lesson: A second factor means one person's mistake doesn't become a disaster for the whole club.

root.title: A Trustworthy Club Admin
root.desc: You fixed the root causes, disabled old accounts, have a working backup, and the club still has nearly as many members as before.

rebuilder.title: The Architect Who Started Over
rebuilder.desc: You took the most expensive path — a full rebuild — and still caught the new vulnerabilities that came with the rush. The system is secure, but membership is not the same.

honest.title: Honest but Bruised
honest.desc: The club took a serious hit, but you told members the truth. The trust that remains is the foundation for a comeback.

survivor.title: A Survivor Who Learned
survivor.desc: The club website is still running and the critical holes are closed — even if there were costs along the way.

nomfa.title: Strong on Fixes, Forgot the Second Layer
nomfa.desc: Old accounts and backups are handled, but admin accounts still rely on a password alone. The remaining risk is a human one.

cover.title: Covered It Up and Lost the Trust
cover.desc: The system may have been fixed — but not telling members only delayed the damage, and when it hit, it hit harder.

scarred.title: Deep Wounds, Still Standing
scarred.desc: The club's data and funds took serious damage. It's still going, but rebuilding member trust will take a long time.

bleeding.title: Bleeding Out
bleeding.desc: You avoided the problem without fixing the system. The attacker keeps coming back. The club is slowly losing members with no end to the incident in sight.

collapse.title: The Club Had to Disband
collapse.desc: Membership dropped too low for the club to continue. Look back and see which decision caused the biggest drop.

AXES.dL: You tend to keep the club website running first, even when risk remains.
AXES.dR: You're willing to lose users in the short term to secure the system first.
AXES.dM: You strike a reasonable balance between security and keeping the club website running.

AXES.dL: You prefer to verify before acting. The upside is precision; the downside is speed.
AXES.dR: You decide quickly. The upside is stopping incidents fast; the downside is missing things.
AXES.dM: You adjust your pace well to the demands of each situation.

AXES.dL: You tend to prioritize image — which often erodes user trust later.
AXES.dR: You tell users the truth, even when it stings in the short term.
AXES.dM: You haven't faced many situations that forced a clear communication choice yet.

AXES.dL: You tend to choose the fast fix, which sometimes leaves the root cause untouched.
AXES.dR: You think about root causes and long-term consequences.
AXES.dM: You mix quick patches with root-cause fixes.
